summary: Specifies how PPP is used over SONET and SDH optical circuits. It replaced RFC 1619.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to send ordinary computer messages down fast fiber-optic telephone lines, packed up neatly so the other end can unpack them.

questions: how does ppp work over sonet
what is the path signal label for ppp
subtitle: How PPP frames ride inside SONET/SDH optical circuits, with a self-synchronous scrambler to keep the line safe.

tldr.problem: PPP needed a defined way to run over SONET/SDH point-to-point circuits, and RFC 1619 had been found to let malicious users craft packets that cause synchronization problems on those links.
tldr.mechanism: HDLC-like framed PPP octets are mapped into the SONET STS-SPE or SDH Higher Order VC and scrambled with an X**43 + 1 self-synchronous scrambler, with Path Signal Label 22 marking the payload.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1619, mainly by adding scrambling and a Security Considerations section.

today: RFC 2615 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1619.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
PPP was designed as a standard method of communicating over point-to-point links. SONET/SDH links are point-to-point circuits by definition, so PPP suits them. The RFC treats SONET and SDH as equivalent for this purpose: apart from terminology, the differences are inconsequential, and it lists the equivalent terms side by side (for example STS-3c-SPE is VC-4 in SDH).

The supported payloads are restricted to four: STS-3c-SPE (VC-4), STS-12c-SPE (VC-4-4c), STS-48c-SPE (VC-4-16c) and STS-192c-SPE (VC-4-64c). The RFC uses the RFC 2119 requirement keywords.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is a way for two computers to talk over a single wire. SONET and SDH are fast fibre lines that are exactly that kind of wire.

sections.title: Physical Layer Requirements
sections.content:
PPP sees SONET/SDH as octet-oriented synchronous full-duplex links. The PPP octet stream, in HDLC-like framing, is mapped into the SONET STS-SPE or SDH Higher Order VC with octet boundaries aligned. The sender works in a fixed order: IP, PPP, FCS generation, byte stuffing, scrambling, then SONET/SDH framing. The receiver reverses it.

The Path Signal Label (C2) says what the payload holds. The value 22 (16 hex) means PPP with X^43 + 1 scrambling. For compatibility with RFC 1619 (STS-3c-SPE/VC-4 only), an implementation may offer a scrambler on/off switch. If so, scrambling MUST default to enabled, and with scrambling off the label is 207 (CF hex). The Multiframe Indicator (H4) is unused and MUST be zero.

PPP does not require control signals, though using them when available can give more functionality and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are packed in a set order, like folding a letter, putting it in an envelope and then stamping it. A label on the outside says the stirred-up (scrambled) kind of packing was used.

sections.title: Framing
sections.content: Framing is the one described in RFC 1662, "PPP in HDLC-like Framing". PPP frames are located by row within the SONET STS-SPE or SDH Higher Order VC payload. Frames vary in length, so they are allowed to cross the boundaries between SPE/VC payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages come in different lengths and are simply packed one after another. A long one may spill from one box into the next.

sections.title: The X**43 + 1 Scrambler
sections.content:
The entire payload, meaning the SPE/VC minus the path overhead and any fixed stuff, is scrambled with a self-synchronous scrambler of polynomial X**43 + 1. The transmitter has a 43-bit shift register whose output is XORed with the unscrambled data, and the result is fed back into the register. The receiver feeds the incoming scrambled data into its own 43-bit register and XORs it with the same data to recover the original.

Bit order matters. The HDLC FCS is calculated least significant bit first, but scrambling is done most significant bit first. The scrambler runs continuously across the payload bytes, skipping path overhead and fixed stuff, and its state is not reset per frame. The transmitter picks the initial seed at random to improve operational security. As a result, the first 43 transmitted bits after startup or reframe are not descrambled correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The scrambler mixes each new bit with one from 43 steps earlier, like a secret handshake the receiver can undo. The first few bits after a restart come out garbled while it catches up.

sections.title: Configuration Details
sections.content:
Apart from FCS length, the standard LCP sync configuration defaults apply. For STS-3c-SPE/VC-4 the RFC recommends the Magic Number option, no Address and Control Field Compression, and no Protocol Field Compression. At STS-12c-SPE/VC-4-4c and above, address and control field compression and protocol field compression are NOT RECOMMENDED, and Magic Number stays RECOMMENDED.

The 32-bit FCS MUST be used at all rates, with one exception: for STS-3c-SPE/VC-4 only, the 16-bit FCS MAY be used, though 32-bit is RECOMMENDED. FCS length is set by provisioning and is not negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends agree ahead of time on the settings. The error-check length is chosen by the people who set up the link, not negotiated on the fly.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 1619
sections.content:
Scrambling is the major change from RFC 1619. That RFC was operationally found to let malicious users generate packets with bit patterns that could create low-transition-density synchronization problems, emulate the SDH set-reset scrambler pattern, and replicate the STM-N frame alignment word. Predicting the scrambler output needs the 43-bit state at the start and every byte scrambled since. The RFC puts the chance of guessing correctly at 1/2**43, with an extra 1/127 for staying aligned, giving a probability of 9e-16, which it calls reasonably secure. It notes the scrambler is also used for ATM over SONET/SDH.

A known remaining issue is bandwidth: a user can fill packets with flag or escape characters and cause up to a 100% increase in the bandwidth needed. Other changes from RFC 1619 are updated terminology, the restriction to the four listed payloads, the C2 value 22, and the requirement for a 32-bit FCS except at STS-3c-SPE/VC-4.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, a troublemaker could write messages that looked like the line's own control signals. Stirring the bits makes that practically impossible to do on purpose.
